messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 66
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Midwife
  trauma_type: Military
  pcl5: 74

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being Watched: Feeling watched or observed, Male Presence: Being alone with men, Authority Figures: People in uniform
  Maladaptive Strategies: Overworking: I throw myself into work or tasks to keep my mind occupied, Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person, Hypervigilance towards people: vigilant for dangerous people
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Anita Patel is a 66-year-old midwife who came to treatment after months of pressure from her husband and one of the younger nurses on her unit, both of whom had noticed that she seemed unable to settle even during ordinary shifts. She had served in the military decades earlier, and when she speaks about that period she does so in clipped, practical fragments, as if keeping to the facts might contain what still lives in her body. The event she returns to happened while she was posted on base and working in a medical setting where rank and gender shaped every interaction. She recalls being cornered in a storage area by a man in uniform, acutely aware of the enclosed room, the sound of boots in the corridor, and the feeling that she was being observed and evaluated even before he moved close. What remains most vivid is not a full story told in sequence, but the sense of a male body blocking the exit, the authority in the uniform, and the conviction that no one would intervene.

In the years after leaving the military, Anita built a life that looked solid from the outside. She married, stayed in healthcare, and became known as a highly dependable midwife, the one who would pick up an extra call shift and remain calm in emergencies. Yet the situations that most closely resembled parts of the trauma never stopped carrying a charge. If she is alone in a room with a man, even a colleague she has known for years, her body reacts before she can reason with it. A security guard pausing at the nurses’ station, a hospital administrator in a formal uniform, or the unmistakable sensation that someone is standing behind her watching her charting can make her go instantly on guard. Sudden movements from other people—someone reaching past her for supplies, a male resident stepping quickly into her path—jolt her into the same tense readiness. In those moments she is scanning faces, positions, exits, unable to relax even when she knows perfectly well she is in a hospital and not in the military anymore.

That constant sense of threat has shaped the way she gets through her days. Anita keeps herself moving almost relentlessly, volunteering for admissions, reorganizing supply carts, staying late to finish notes that could wait until morning, because if she is occupied every minute there is less room for the raw alertness to break through. She has also made quiet rules for herself that she rarely says out loud: she avoids being alone with any man whenever she can, asks a nurse to stay in the room if a male physician needs to discuss a case, and times her walk to the parking garage so she leaves alongside others. Around people she does not know well, especially men, she watches closely for who is standing where, who is approaching, whose movements seem abrupt. To Anita this does not feel excessive; it feels like the only sensible way to prevent herself from being trapped off guard.

Over time those strategies have begun to tighten her world rather than steady it. Because she throws herself into work, she is almost always in the hospital, and the hospital is full of the very situations that set her off: male residents crossing in and out of patient rooms, security staff in uniform, orderlies appearing suddenly at her shoulder, the frequent feeling of being watched in busy corridors and at central desks. Because she insists on never being alone with another person, she is constantly arranging her day around who is present, which means she notices every moment when she might be left with a man in an office, elevator, or supply room. The more she monitors for dangerous people and keeps herself surrounded, the more quickly her attention catches on male presence, uniforms, and the sense of observation. At work this has become visible. She now chooses tasks based less on clinical need than on where other women are stationed, and she has passed over supervisory duties that would require closed-door meetings with male administrators.

Her husband has seen the same pattern at home in a different form. Anita paces from chore to chore, unable to sit still through an evening without finding something to clean, fold, or prepare. If a repairman is scheduled, she asks a neighbor to come over. If someone moves suddenly near her, she startles and fixes her eyes on them at once. What frightened her most, she said in the first session, was not only that she was always braced, but that she had come to live as if danger could step out of any ordinary moment. She finally sought help after snapping at a male obstetrics resident who approached her too quickly from behind while she was charting; afterward she was ashamed, but also shaken by how immediate and absolute her reaction had been. Anita says she wants to keep working, and she wants to be able to walk through her own workplace without feeling hunted. Most of all, she is afraid that if she does not get help now, this vigilant, overworked version of her life will be the only one she has left.
